intro: Frank Lévy plays Chopin’s Nocturne in E♭ major, Op. 9 No. 2, recorded for Musopen’s project to set the music free. The melody returns with more elaborate ornamentation each time, and a short cadenza follows.

sections.label: A · A sixth begins the song
sections.mNote: B♭ rises to G above the recurring left-hand chords

sections.label: B · B♭ above an E♮ bass
sections.mNote: The familiar melody is harmonised with a diminished seventh.

sections.label: C · A♭ minor, ascent to cadenza
sections.mNote: Minor chords lead to octaves and the cadenza.

sections.label: Coda · E♭ major after the cadenza
sections.mNote: The piano plays soft, rolled chords in E♭ major.

cues.title: Opening upbeat and bar 1
cues.text: The melody begins on a single B♭ and rises a sixth to G. The G is held while the left hand plays a bass note and two chords on each beat. The tune then descends, with a short rise on the way.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), upbeat and bar 1; Mutopia transcription: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Varied return of the opening phrase
cues.text: In bars 5–8 the first phrase returns, varied. The long G is now ornamented, and E♭ also carries added small notes. The bass repeats its pattern from bars 1–4 while the right hand plays an elaborated version of the melody.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bars 5–8, varied restatement of bars 1–4. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Musopen Chopin recording, 2014
cues.text: In 2014 Lévy joined Musopen’s recording of Chopin’s complete works, which was released into the public domain. He had studied with Leon Fleisher in Baltimore and taught at Juilliard. His recording of the E♭-major Nocturne is part of that collection.
cues.evidence: Lévy’s 2014 Musopen collaboration, teaching and Fleisher studies: https://www.sjsu.edu/music/faculty-staff/directory/frank-levy.php. Set Chopin Free’s public-domain purpose: https://culture.pl/en/article/set-chopin-free

cues.title: Coda, bars 25–26
cues.text: The coda begins with the melody on E♭. Underneath, A♭-minor chords sound before E♭ major returns. The bass holds E♭ through both harmonies.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bars 25–26, headed Coda: A♭-minor and E♭-major harmony over E♭. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Senza tempo passage, bar 32
cues.text: At bar 32, marked senza tempo, the regular beat no longer governs the phrase. High octaves are held above a B♭ dominant chord while the four-note figure C♭–B♭–C♮–A♮ repeats several times. The right hand then plays a descending run.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bar 32: senza tempo, held dominant harmony and repeated C♭–B♭–C♮–A♮ figure. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of Tempo I in E♭
cues.text: The first tempo returns with E♭-major chords played softly. The right hand rises to G again, now as part of the accompaniment. The piece ends on three chords marked ppp.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bars 33–34: Tempo I, pianissimo, then pianississimo closing chords. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Bass rises from E♭ to E♮
transitions.from: A · A sixth begins the song
transitions.to: B · B♭ above an E♮ bass
transitions.how: In bars 18–19 the bass moves from E♭ to E♮. With G, B♭ and D♭ above it, the new note forms a diminished seventh. The melody leaps to B♭ and descends through A♮ to G. Beneath it the left hand continues its bass-and-chord pattern through the diminished-seventh harmony.

transitions.title: A♭ minor before the cadenza
transitions.from: B · B♭ above an E♮ bass
transitions.to: C · A♭ minor, ascent to cadenza
transitions.how: The bass drops to A♭ under an A♭-minor chord, then returns to E♭ major. Above it, the tune turns around E♭ and F. Chopin next writes con forza, then stretto. The right hand climbs into octaves, and the measured accompaniment stops for the cadenza.

transitions.title: B♭ dominant resolves under the falling run
transitions.from: C · A♭ minor, ascent to cadenza
transitions.to: Coda · E♭ major after the cadenza
transitions.how: The cadenza runs above a held B♭ dominant seventh. The right hand descends, and its last C and D lead to E♭. The bass takes E♭ underneath, the first tempo returns, and both hands play a soft rolled tonic chord.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
